blocks.how_it_works: Rhode Island has no general UTC-style certification of trust statute. Instead, R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-4-27 provides a real-property affidavit or memorandum of trust that serves a similar function for recording purposes. The memorandum must include: the trust name; every settlor and original trustee; original instrument and amendment or restatement dates; current trustees; whether trustees may act without beneficiary consent and their authority over conveyances, mortgages, leases, restrictions, easements, and other real-estate interests, with relevant trust provisions attached; whether the trust limits those powers; revocation or termination status and any power to convey property to carry it out; trustee replacement and successor appointment method; termination timing and manner; revocability and circumstances of irrevocability; and any applicable settlor death date and place. The affidavit must be executed by every settlor or every current trustee. Recording is optional at creation, amendment, or revocation but mandatory for trustee transfers or mortgages of real property.

faq.q: Does Rhode Island have a statutory certification of trust like UTC states?
faq.a: No. Rhode Island has not adopted the Uniform Trust Code and has no general UTC-style certification of trust statute. The closest analog is R.I. Gen. Laws Section 18-3-3, which safeguards persons dealing with trustees. For real property purposes, R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-4-27 provides a real-property affidavit or memorandum of trust that serves a similar function. This memorandum is more detailed than a standard UTC certification, requiring attachment of relevant trust provisions regarding real estate authority.

faq.q: What must a Rhode Island real-property memorandum of trust contain?
faq.a: Under R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-4-27, the memorandum must include: the trust name; every settlor and original trustee; original instrument and amendment or restatement dates; current trustees; whether trustees may act without beneficiary consent and their authority over conveyances, mortgages, leases, restrictions, easements, and other real-estate interests; whether the trust limits those powers; revocation or termination status; trustee replacement and successor appointment method; termination timing and manner; revocability and circumstances of irrevocability; and any applicable settlor death date and place.

faq.q: Who must sign a Rhode Island memorandum of trust?
faq.a: R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-4-27 requires the affidavit to be executed by every settlor or every current trustee, an all-or-all requirement that is stricter than the UTC's any-trustee rule. The statute does not require a notary, witness, or attorney authentication for the memorandum itself. However, separate recording requirements for particular instruments may apply. For real property transactions, the memorandum or trust instrument must be recorded. Notarization is recommended though not required by the trust statute itself.

faq.q: How does Rhode Island protect third parties who rely on a memorandum of trust?
faq.a: Under R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-4-27, a third party without actual contrary knowledge may rely on the statements in the memorandum of trust. The statute does not contain a specific bad-faith demand provision or damages rule comparable to UTC states. The reliance protection is limited to third parties without actual contrary knowledge, without the UTC's additional enforcement and bad-faith-demand provisions. The statute also does not limit the right to obtain the trust instrument in judicial proceedings.

blocks.common_mistakes: A common mistake is treating Rhode Island as a UTC state and citing a certification of trust statute that does not exist. Rhode Island relies on R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-4-27 for real-property affidavits and Section 18-3-3 as the closest analog for safeguarding persons dealing with trustees. Failing to attach relevant trust provisions regarding real estate authority under Section 34-4-27 is another frequent error, as the statute requires these provisions to be attached. The all-or-all signer requirement means that omitting any settlor or current trustee invalidates the memorandum. Assuming the memorandum provides the same reliance protections as a UTC certification of trust is incorrect, as Rhode Island's statutory framework is less comprehensive.
blocks.state_notes: Rhode Island has not adopted the Uniform Trust Code, relying instead on common law and scattered statutory provisions in Title 18. This makes Rhode Island's trust law less codified and more dependent on judicial precedent than most other states. Rhode Island repealed the Rule Against Perpetuities in 1999, allowing perpetual trusts and dynasty trusts. The state repealed the centuries-old law prohibiting property owners from shielding assets in a trust from creditors in 1999. Rhode Island imposes state income tax on trust income for resident trusts at rates of 3.75% to 5.99%, among the higher rates in New England. The Uniform Prudent Investor Act at R.I. Gen. Laws Ch. 18-15 governs trust investment. The common law framework provides flexibility but less statutory certainty and guidance for trustees and beneficiaries. R.I. Gen. Laws Section 18-3-3 safeguards persons dealing with trustees and serves as the closest analog to a certification of trust statute.
